chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa al-Ash'ari, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id al-Ahwazi, from al-Nadhr ibn Suwayd, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said: Did Allah not cease to be Willing? He said: The one who wills cannot be (considered as such) except that what is willed is (present) with Him. (Instead say:) Allah never ceased being Knowledgeable and Powerful and then He willed.

key_terms.ثُمَّ أَرَادَ: Then He willed (indicating a subsequent act or distinction)
key_terms.لِمُرَادٍ: That which is willed (the object of will)
key_terms.مُرِيدًا: Willing (one who has a specific will or desire)

ai.seo_question: What is the relationship between God's eternal knowledge and His act of willing in Shia theology?
ai.summary: In this narration from Al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the theological nuance of Divine Will by distinguishing between God's eternal attributes and His specific volition. He explains that 'Will' necessitates an object of will coexisting with the Willer, thereby affirming that God’s knowledge and power are eternal, and His act of willing is not a new occurrence but a manifestation of His eternal purpose. This aligns with the Shia scholarly emphasis on the unity of God's attributes, ensuring that His will is not seen as a temporal change in His essence.

en.ammaar-muslim: 2. [2/351] al-Kafi: Muhammad b. Yahya al-Attar from Ahmad b. Muhammad b. Isa al-Ash’ari from al-Husayn b. Sai’d al-Ahwazi from al-Nadhr b. Suwayd from A’sim b. Humayd from Abi Abdillah (as). He (A’sim) said:

I said: Allah never stopped willing? He said: The one who wills cannot be (considered as such) except that what is willed is (present) with Him. (Instead say:) Allah never stopped being knowledgeable and powerful and then He willed.
